questions.question: Your API uses cookie-based auth and must be called from https://app.example.com. Which CORS setup is correct?
options: An explicit origin allow-list containing https://app.example.com, with credentials: true
Reflect whatever Origin header arrives, with credentials: true
No CORS middleware; cookies make CORS unnecessary
questions.explanation: Browsers reject a wildcard origin with credentials, and reflecting any origin lets every site make authenticated requests. An explicit allow-list is the safe choice.

questions.question: Your app runs behind one load balancer and you add express-rate-limit without setting trust proxy. What happens?
options: Every request appears to come from the load balancer's IP, so all users share one rate-limit bucket
Rate limiting is applied per user ID automatically
Each request gets a random IP, so nothing is limited
questions.explanation: req.ip is the proxy's address unless trust proxy is configured. Setting it to the hop count (e.g. 1) makes req.ip the real client IP.

questions.question: Why is app.set("trust proxy", true) risky on a server behind a single proxy?
options: Express trusts the whole X-Forwarded-For chain, so clients can spoof their IP and dodge IP-based rate limits
questions.explanation: Trusting every hop means the left-most, client-controlled value is used as req.ip. Trusting exactly the known number of proxies prevents spoofing.

questions.question: Which API is NOT exposed to classic CSRF attacks?
options: One that authenticates with a session cookie using sameSite: "none"
One that changes data on GET requests with cookie auth
One that only accepts a Bearer token in the Authorization header
One that stores a JWT in a cookie without sameSite
questions.explanation: CSRF relies on the browser attaching credentials automatically. A malicious site cannot make the browser add an Authorization header, so Bearer-token-only APIs avoid classic CSRF.
